name: Hay fever (allergic rhinitis)
definition: Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen, also called seasonal allergic rhinitis.
overview: Hay fever is a common allergy that causes sneezing, coughing and itchy eyes. It is an allergic reaction to pollen from plants, usually when pollen touches the mouth, nose, eyes or throat. Unlike a cold, its symptoms can last for weeks or months. The NHS says there is no cure, but symptoms can be eased.
causes: An allergic reaction to pollen from plants.
Pollen from trees, grasses and weeds is the usual trigger.
riskFactors: Allergies tend to run in families, and a parent with an allergic disease raises a child's risk.
One review also noted antibiotic use, air pollution and parental smoking as possible factors.
signs: A clinician may find a crease across the bridge of the nose, open-mouth breathing or dark shadows under the eyes.
complications: Sinusitis is the most common complication of persistent rhinitis.
Allergic rhinitis is a risk factor for developing asthma.
Poorly controlled hay fever can worsen existing asthma.
diagnosis: Diagnosis usually starts with a physical examination and a history of symptoms. Skin or blood tests are sometimes added.
treatment: A pharmacist can recommend antihistamine tablets, drops or nasal sprays, and steroid nasal sprays. If these do not help, a GP may refer the person for immunotherapy, which gradually builds tolerance to pollen.
prevention: The NHS says hay fever cannot be prevented, but symptoms can be eased. Allergy UK suggests checking pollen forecasts and showering and changing clothes after being outdoors.
seekCare: A pharmacist is the usual first contact for hay fever treatment. A routine GP appointment is the route if treatment has not helped, or if symptoms affect everyday tasks or treatment causes side effects. Wheeze, breathlessness or worsening asthma need prompt medical attention, through NHS 111 or the GP the same day. Call 999 for severe difficulty breathing.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of hay fever?
sections.body:
The NHS lists sneezing, a runny or blocked nose, and itchy or watery eyes as common signs of hay fever. An itchy throat is also common, and some people have tiredness, headaches or a loss of smell. Allergy UK adds itching in the ears, fatigue and poor sleep to the list.

Hay fever can look like a cold, but a cold usually clears within one to two weeks. Hay fever symptoms tend to last for weeks or months. Local NHS pages say symptoms typically peak from late March to September.

People with asthma may notice chest tightness, wheeze or breathlessness during the pollen season. NHS sources describe wheeze, shortness of breath or worsening asthma as needing prompt medical attention.

sections.heading: What causes hay fever, and when is it worst?
sections.body:
Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen from plants. The reaction usually happens when pollen touches the mouth, nose, eyes or throat. MedlinePlus, a United States source, names pollen from trees, grasses and ragweed. Allergy UK describes hay fever as driven by tree, grass and weed pollen.

Tree pollen is usually released first, from late March to mid-May, followed by grass and then weed pollen. Weed pollen runs longer, with peak levels often in July and August. Some people react to one type of pollen and then feel better, while others are affected by several. Some people are allergic to both tree and grass pollen and have symptoms for most of the spring and summer.

Warm, calm, sunny weather raises pollen counts, while cold or cloudy spells reduce them. Rain clears pollen from the air, so counts tend to fall on wet days.

sections.heading: How is hay fever diagnosed?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says diagnosis usually starts with a physical examination and a history of symptoms. Skin or blood tests are sometimes added, including blood tests that measure allergy-related substances. One patient information sheet says tests are usually not required.

Local NHS pathways describe diagnosis as a clinical assessment, because the symptoms are usually typical. One formulary lists a runny nose, sneezing, a blocked nose on both sides and itchy eyes as the typical group of symptoms. A clinician may look for a crease across the nose, open-mouth breathing and dark shadows under the eyes.

A review suggests an allergy specialist may be consulted when symptoms persist despite the best medical treatment. A Devon pathway lists symptoms on one side only, polyps, persistent pus-like discharge or blood staining as reasons for urgent referral to an ear, nose and throat specialist.

sections.heading: How is hay fever treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no cure for hay fever, but symptoms can be eased. Pharmacists can recommend antihistamine tablets, drops or nasal sprays, and steroid nasal sprays. One local NHS page says non-drowsy antihistamines such as cetirizine, loratadine and fexofenadine are the usual first choice. Older antihistamines such as chlorphenamine are more likely to cause sleepiness.

Steroid nasal sprays can take a few days to work and may be combined with an antihistamine at first. MedlinePlus describes nasal corticosteroid sprays as the most effective of the main options. Eye drops containing sodium cromoglicate need regular use to be effective.

Local NHS guidance says GPs generally no longer prescribe oral antihistamines, steroid nasal sprays or these eye drops for hay fever. They are therefore usually bought from a pharmacy, and local rules vary. If standard medicines do not help, a GP may refer the person for immunotherapy, which gradually builds tolerance to pollen. The NHS says immunotherapy is usually started a few months before the pollen season.

sections.heading: Living with hay fever and getting help
sections.body:
The NHS suggests wearing wraparound sunglasses, showering after going outdoors and keeping windows shut. Putting petroleum jelly around the nostrils can catch pollen, the NHS says. Allergy UK recommends checking pollen forecasts and staying indoors on high-count days. It also advises showering and changing clothes after being outdoors. Allergy UK says a daily non-sedating antihistamine works for most people.

A pharmacist is the usual first contact for hay fever treatment. Allergy UK advises seeing a GP or pharmacist if symptoms do not improve with treatment or last more than two weeks. Local NHS advice says to seek help sooner if symptoms affect everyday tasks or treatment causes side effects. Wheeze, breathlessness or worsening asthma need prompt medical attention, through NHS 111 or the GP the same day.

faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for hay fever and it cannot be prevented, but symptoms can be eased. Pharmacists can recommend antihistamines and steroid nasal sprays. If these do not work, a GP may refer the person for immunotherapy, which gradually builds tolerance to pollen. Allergy UK says a daily non-sedating antihistamine works for most people.

faqs.q: How can hay fever be told apart from a cold?
faqs.a: Hay fever and a cold can look similar. A cold usually clears within one to two weeks, while hay fever symptoms tend to last for weeks or months. Hay fever commonly brings itchy or watery eyes and an itchy throat. Allergy UK advises seeing a GP or pharmacist if symptoms last more than two weeks.

People with asthma may notice chest tightness, wheeze or breathlessness during the pollen season. Allergic rhinitis is a risk factor for developing asthma, and poorly controlled hay fever can worsen existing asthma. Wheeze, breathlessness or worsening asthma need prompt medical attention, through NHS 111 or the GP the same day.

faqs.q: When is the hay fever season?
faqs.a: Tree pollen is usually released first, from late March to mid-May, followed by grass and then weed pollen. Weed pollen peaks often in July and August. Some people react to several types and have symptoms for most of the spring and summer. Warm, calm, sunny weather raises pollen counts, while rain tends to lower them.

faqs.q: Does hay fever run in families?
faqs.a: Allergies tend to run in families, and a 2024 review reports that parents with allergic diseases raise a child's risk. The review also noted antibiotic use, air pollution and parental smoking as other possible factors. Hay fever itself is an allergic reaction to pollen from plants.
